svg.aria-label: Power-on sequence of an i.MX95 board, from the PMIC to the BootROM reading the first container
svg.title: From power-on to the first instruction

g.text: ◂ A55 cluster and M7 held in reset

svg.text: Power-up timeline · simplified, not to scale

g.text: Board unpowered. Every rail is at 0 V and nothing on the SoC is running.
Input power reaches the PMIC. Its one-time-programmable memory (OTP) holds the rail order, the voltages and the delays
The PMIC brings up the SoC rails in the order its OTP sets: the always-on domain first, then the core logic rails,
then the analog and I/O supplies. Some steps may overlap.
Then the DRAM rails, in the order the memory standard requires. The DRAM has power from now on, but nothing can use it
until it has been initialized and trained (part 3).
The 24 MHz crystal oscillator starts and settles. The SoC's clocks are derived from it.
With every rail in regulation, the PMIC releases the power-on reset, POR_B. The SoC leaves reset and latches the
The BootROM starts executing on the Cortex-M33, the boot core, not on the A55. The secure enclave (ELE) runs its own
ROM. The A55 cluster and the M7 stay in reset.
The ROM works only from on-chip memory: its stack and data sit in a reserved part of the M33's TCM, and images go to
their load addresses in on-chip RAM. The DDR is powered, but still locked.
The ROM reads the boot mode, latched from the pins at reset, and the boot fuses. Here they select the SD card.
The ROM brings up the SD controller and the card, starting at the slow identification clock the SD specification
requires, and reads from offset 32 KiB.
Container #1 starts at 32 KiB. The ROM copies its header into on-chip memory, then hands the NXP-signed ELE firmware
to the ELE, which verifies it and starts running it. Part 2 opens this container.
